questions.q: How is a QAOA run's approximation ratio defined?
options: The expected cost achieved divided by the true optimal cost
The number of qubits divided by circuit depth
The number of layers p divided by 2
The total number of gates divided by the number of measurements
questions.explain: Approximation ratio r = (expected cost achieved) / (true optimal cost), with r=1.0 meaning the circuit's expected measured cost exactly matches the best possible answer.

questions.q: On the 4-cycle Max-Cut problem (true optimum = 4), what approximation ratio did direct simulation find at depth p=1?
questions.explain: The best depth-1 expected cost found was ≈2.9996 out of a true optimum of 4, giving an approximation ratio of ≈0.75.

questions.q: What approximation ratio did depth p=2 achieve on the same 4-cycle problem, and what does this demonstrate?
options: ≈0.9999, demonstrating that doubling the depth took this problem from 75% of optimal to essentially optimal
≈0.50, demonstrating that more depth made the result worse
≈0.75, identical to p=1, demonstrating depth has no effect
Exactly 2.0, demonstrating the approximation ratio can exceed 1.0
questions.explain: Direct simulation with a refined 4-parameter search found an expected cost of ≈3.9998, giving an approximation ratio of ≈0.9999 -- essentially the true optimum, up from ≈0.75 at depth 1.

questions.q: What is the practical tradeoff that limits how much QAOA depth can be used on real quantum hardware today, even though theory says higher p converges to the true optimum?
options: Each additional layer adds more gates, and since every physical gate has some error probability (typically 99.0%-99.9% fidelity), deeper circuits accumulate more total error, which can outweigh the theoretical benefit of added expressiveness
Deeper circuits always require fewer classical optimization parameters, which paradoxically hurts performance
Quantum hardware physically cannot execute more than one layer at a time
There is no real tradeoff; higher p is always strictly better on all hardware
questions.explain: While QAOA's achievable expected cost provably converges to the optimum as p grows in theory, each extra layer's extra gates compound hardware error on noisy real devices -- a depth-vs-noise tradeoff the lesson explicitly refuses to wave away.

questions.q: What classical-optimizer technique was used to find the depth p=2 result of ≈3.9998, given that p=2 has 4 tunable parameters?
options: A coarse grid search over the 4-parameter space followed by local coordinate-wise refinement
An exact closed-form algebraic solution requiring no search at all
Random guessing with no structured search
A gradient descent method requiring the parameter-shift rule
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly describes using a coarse grid search over (gamma_1, beta_1, gamma_2, beta_2) followed by coordinate-wise local refinement -- the same gradient-free classical-optimizer pattern introduced in Lesson 8.
